title: URL Shortener Deep Dive
description: Go beyond the basics — analytics pipelines, custom aliases, link expiration, and geographic distribution for a production-grade URL shortener.

segments.text: You can build a basic URL shortener in a weekend. But building one that handles billions of redirects, tracks analytics in real time, and works globally? That requires serious system design thinking. Let's take this to production grade.

Every click on a short URL is a data point. Who clicked, when, from where, what device, what referrer. This analytics data is incredibly valuable. But recording it synchronously during the redirect would add latency. Users expect redirects to be instant.

The solution is an asynchronous analytics pipeline. On each click, fire the redirect immediately and publish a click event to Kafka. A downstream consumer processes these events, enriches them with geolocation data, and writes to an analytics database like ClickHouse.
segments.thought_prompt: Why use Kafka instead of writing directly to the analytics database?

segments.text: Users want custom short URLs like bit.ly/my-brand. Custom aliases add a uniqueness constraint: you must check the alias doesn't already exist before allowing it. This requires a lookup against your entire URL database, which needs to be fast.

For generated short codes, you need a strategy to avoid collisions. You can pre-generate a pool of unique codes using a counter service, or hash the long URL and check for collisions. A counter-based approach with base62 encoding is simplest and guarantees uniqueness.

Links should expire. Without expiration, your database grows forever and old links consume resources. Implement TTL-based expiration: store an expiry timestamp with each URL. On redirect, check if the link has expired. Run a background job to clean up expired entries.

The read-to-write ratio for a URL shortener is extreme — maybe 100 to 1. Most short URLs are accessed thousands of times but created once. This screams for aggressive caching. Put popular URLs in Redis, and you can serve redirects in under a millisecond.

A URL shortener serving global users needs geographic distribution. Put redirect servers and caches in multiple regions. A user in Tokyo shouldn't wait for a round trip to Virginia. Use DNS-based routing or anycast to direct users to the nearest point of presence.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you keep the cache in Tokyo consistent with the database in Virginia?

segments.text: For the URL mapping store, you want fast key-value lookups. DynamoDB, Cassandra, or even a sharded MySQL setup work well. The access pattern is simple: given a short code, return the long URL. No complex queries, no joins. This is a textbook key-value workload.

Protect your creation endpoint with rate limiting. Without it, a single bad actor could generate millions of short URLs and exhaust your code space. Limit creation by API key, IP address, or user account. Allow generous redirect rates but strict creation limits.

A production URL shortener combines key-value storage, caching, async analytics, global distribution, and abuse prevention. It's deceptively simple on the surface but touches almost every system design concept we've covered. That's why it's a favorite interview question.
